prompt: Most requests finish in 20 ms, but a small group representing 2% of requests takes 3 seconds. Which report best exposes that slow experience?

options.text: Report only the median because it describes every user's experience
options.explanation: Incorrect. The median can remain fast while a minority experiences very slow responses.

options.text: Average the fast and slow durations without weighting their request counts
options.explanation: Incorrect. That treats the two groups as equally common and still does not expose a tail threshold.

options.text: Report the median and p99 alongside the mean
options.explanation: Correct. The median describes typical requests; p99 lies within this slowest 2%, revealing the tail that the mean can soften.

options.text: Replace all percentiles with the mean
options.explanation: Incorrect. The mean combines durations into one number and can hide how differently requests behave.

workedExample: Sort the requests conceptually. More than half are fast, so the median is fast. The slow group occupies the final 2% of positions, which includes the 99th percentile. A mean between the two durations does not mean any actual request took that long.

prompt: You run 20 API servers. Each reports its own p99 latency every minute, and your dashboard shows the **average of the 20 p99 values** as "fleet p99". One server is badly degraded. What is wrong with this metric?

options.text: Nothing; averaging p99s gives the fleet p99 when servers get equal traffic
options.explanation: Incorrect. Percentiles aren't linear, so they can't be averaged even with equal traffic. The true fleet p99 depends on the combined distribution of all requests.

options.text: It should use the median of the p99s instead of the mean
options.explanation: Incorrect. The median of p99s would hide the degraded server even more effectively. Any statistic computed over per-server percentiles is still not the fleet percentile.

options.text: p99 is the wrong metric; use the mean, which can be averaged
options.explanation: Incorrect. Means can be combined, but they hide tail latency, which is the thing you need to see here. The fix is correct aggregation, not a worse metric.

options.text: Percentiles can't be averaged; you must merge the underlying histograms and compute p99 from the combined distribution
options.explanation: Correct. If one server's requests are all slow, they can make up the whole of the fleet's slowest 1%, so the true fleet p99 is that server's latency, while the average of p99s dilutes it with 19 healthy values. Merge histogram buckets (e.g. Prometheus `histogram_quantile` over summed buckets) instead.

workedExample: Imagine equally loaded servers where one server's requests are all slow. That server can contribute more than the fleet's slowest 1%, even though its p99 is only one of twenty dashboard inputs. Averaging those twenty inputs dilutes the slow server instead of finding the slowest requests. Merge compatible histogram counts, then estimate the percentile from the combined distribution; bucket resolution limits accuracy.

prompt: You're asked to produce a trustworthy p99 latency figure for a service before launch. Which practices help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use scheduled-start latency correction (e.g. `wrk2`), or a suitable open-loop generator that accounts for delayed sends
options.explanation: Correct. Measuring from intended send times includes waiting caused by a stall. wrk2 uses this correction even when actual sending falls behind its planned rate; appropriate open-loop tests can also expose the delayed demand.

options.text: Use a closed-loop tester where each client waits for a response before sending the next request
options.explanation: Incorrect. During a stall a closed-loop client stops sending, so the requests that *would* have suffered the stall are never measured. This is coordinated omission and it flatters the tail.

options.text: Record latencies into histograms on every host and merge the histograms before computing p99
options.explanation: Correct. Percentiles must come from the combined distribution. Merged histograms estimate the fleet-wide p99 from the combined distribution; accuracy depends on bucket resolution.

options.text: Report the average of each host's p99
options.explanation: Incorrect. Percentiles can't be averaged; one degraded host can be hidden almost completely.

options.text: Also measure from the client side, not only inside the server's request handler
options.explanation: Correct. Handler timing misses network time, TLS, load balancer hops and time spent queued before the handler starts, which is often where the tail lives.

workedExample:
Consider a 1-second server stall during a test at 1,000 req/s.

```
planned rate: ~1,000 starts during stall
corrected: delay includes intended start
closed loop (10 clients):
            ~10 requests delayed,
            senders paused, rest unseen
```

The closed-loop test records about 100x fewer slow requests, so its p99 looks far better than what real users, who don't politely wait, would see. Use a tester that accounts for intended arrival times, merge histograms with suitable bucket resolution, and measure from the client.
